name: #lecture: The Magic of Boredom
description: How do you get the ideas behind your short stories? Someone had asked the Russian writer Anton Chekhov. Reportedly, Chekhov had responded: “Put your cigarette on this ash-tray and I’ll write a story about it.”This response presents the perfect picture of modern literature that came into existence with the popularisation of print culture and the making of novels and short stories.Classical epics, oral tales, and myths and legends of the past took a great, telescopic view of grand subjects, particularly those of war and romance, in a world full of magic and fantasy populated by gods and kings.This lecture will show how modern literature, shaped by the rhythm of the factory, dominated by clock-time and full of industrial workers and a middle class, turned to everyday themes that resonated with ordinary people, and focused a microscopic lens on the small magic of the cigarette on the ash-tray.About the Speaker Saikat Majumdar is a novelist, critic and educator. name: Designing Your Life, The Stanford Way
description: About the LectureWhat if the life you're living right now is one you drifted into by default, not one you chose?We are born into stories, about success, work, money, relationships, identity and what a good life should look like. Somewhere along the way, those stories start to feel like our own, and a life shaped by default begins to feel like one shaped by choice.Stanford's Designing Your Life offers another way to look at it: life as something you can actively design. That doesn't mean finding one "true" self or one perfect path. It means moving towards self-authorship: questioning the narratives you inherited, imagining different futures, and accepting that there may be more than one life within you worth living.Design turns out to be an unusually useful lens for this, because it doesn't require you to know the answer before you begin. It lets you work with ambiguity, hold several possibilities at once, and experiment rather than predict. In a world where lives are increasingly nonlinear, that may be more useful than having a perfect plan.The session explores:How inherited social narratives quietly become the stories we live byWhy there may be more than one life within us worth livingHow designers work with ambiguity, and why that matters for life decisionsMoving from a life by default to a life by design: question, imagine, prototypeAbout the SpeakerNavyug Mohnot is a Stanford-certified Designing Your Life educator, coach and facilitator, a visiting faculty member at ISB and Ashoka University, and the founder and CEO of QAI Global. name: Can We Make Delhi a Human City?
description: Welcome to Human City Conversations where we have intimate conversations about how cities are built, how they are lived, and who gets to shape them.Conversation 1: HOW DO WE MAKE DELHI A HUMAN CITY?Delhi is a city of contradictions. It has some of India's best public institutions, an expanding metro network, enormous infrastructure projects and a new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 that sets out a vision for how the city should grow and change over the next two decades. And yet, the experience of living in Delhi can be very different.Millions of people spend hours commuting across the city. Walking can feel like an afterthought. Public spaces are often unevenly distributed and poorly connected. For many women, moving through the city comes with a calculation of safety that men may never have to make. And then there is the air. Every winter, Delhi's air pollution becomes a public health crisis forcing a city of millions to think about something as fundamental as whether it is safe to breathe outside.So how can a city with so much planning, infrastructure and investment still struggle with some of the most basic conditions of everyday urban life? Perhaps the problem is not simply how much we build, perhaps we need to ask a more fundamental question:What kind of city are we actually trying to build? And more importantly, who is that city being built for?For the first Human City Conversation, urbanist Jagan Shah joins Ruchita Bansal for an open conversation about Delhi, its future and the gap between the city we plan on paper and the city people actually experience. We'll explore what makes a city genuinely liveable from mobility and housing to public space, safety, air pollution and neighbourhoods and look at what Delhi's new Master Plan for 2047 could mean on the ground.What to ExpectA curated, open conversation between urbanist Jagan Shah and Ruchita BansalA look at Delhi's urban future and what the new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 could mean on the groundA discussion about the gap between the city we plan and the city people actually experienceA closer look at how cities are shaped by policies, infrastructure and development decisionsPerspectives on what makes a city genuinely liveable, accessible and inclusiveA 30 minute Q&A SessionInformal discussion and one on one conversation after the conversationEvent Details📅 Sunday, 11 October 2026🕔 5:00 PM onwards📍 Kunzum Books, GK II, Delhi☕ Your ticket includes one coffee/tea .About the SpeakerJagan Shah is an urbanist, architect and former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), with decades of experience working at the intersection of urban planning, policy, governance and development. He has been closely involved in shaping India's urban policy and planning landscape, including work connected to Delhi's Master Plan, the Smart Cities Mission and other national urban development programmes. His work has involved developing and implementing policies and frameworks that influence how Indian cities grow, transform and respond to the challenges of rapid urbanisation.Over the years, Jagan has worked across urban planning, housing, infrastructure, heritage, governance and institutional development, working with governments and institutions at different levels.His experience spans both the making of plans and policies and the realities of implementing them, making him particularly well placed to examine the gap between the city we envision on paper and the city that people actually experience.About the ModeratorRuchita Bansal is an architect and urban planner with 15 years of experience working on cities, urban development and planning policy. Her work has ranged from developing planning frameworks and regulations to working directly on large-scale urban transformation projects. She was part of the team behind Ayodhya Vision 2047, working on one of India's most complex and rapidly transforming urban environments and seeing first-hand the challenges of translating ambitious plans and visions into reality on the ground.Today, Ruchita is the Creator and Host of The Human City Podcast and the founder of SheCity India, using conversations, research and storytelling to make urban planning more accessible and bring the discussion about cities beyond the professional planning community. Through The Human City, she explores a simple but often overlooked question: what does all this planning mean for the people who actually live in our cities?Note: Attendance implies consent to being filmed for event documentation. If you do not wish to be filmed, please reach out to your curator for the evening, Ruchita. Come curious. Come questioning. Come ready to talk about the city we call home.

name: The FishMarket #2
description: A FishMarket isn't a lecture. It's a room full of concerned citizens trying to solve a problem together.This one is about something we all experience every single day, and almost never stop to actually diagnose.Moving through a city should be simple. And yet an ordinary journey on foot, by bicycle, motorcycle or car routinely becomes an exercise in negotiation. The footpath disappears into parking. The pedestrian steps onto the road. The rider squeezes through a gap that probably shouldn't exist. The car stops wherever space appears. Each decision seems reasonable to the person making it. Together, they produce confusion, delay, and risk.But here's what we rarely ask: is this actually about bad civic sense? name: GFT: October Edition in Defence Colony
description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Defence Colony)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.1st October: Dolan SamantaTemple sculpture is usually read as devotion — divine bodies carved to be worshipped. This session argues it does something more: these images are sites where gender, desire, and authority are negotiated, not just depicted. Taking two ninth-to-eleventh-century carvings of Śiva and Pārvatī from the Nīlakaṇṭha temple at Kālañjara as its central text, and reading them through Puranic myth, Foucault, and Judith Butler's account of gender as performance, Dolan Samanta, a history educator and JNU-trained researcher, asks why Śiva appears nude, enraged, and armed, his sexuality fused with dominance, while Pārvatī appears smaller, modest, at once desired and desiring. The question stone carved a thousand years ago still puts to us: who was permitted power, and who was only expected to receive it?8th October: Tania KapoorMost parents still treat marks as the surest route to a child's future — but school mostly rewards memorising, following instructions, and reproducing the right answer in the right way, exactly the kind of work AI is fastest at absorbing. Tania Kapoor, a Delhi-based child and adolescent psychologist trained at AIIMS, argues that what will actually distinguish children going forward — adaptability, emotional regulation, impulse control, comfort with ambiguity — is precisely what classrooms and busy households keep treating as something to address "later" Grounded in clinical practice, this session asks what parents should be paying attention to now, before later becomes too late.15th October: Dr. Jasleen RanaEvery purchase carries a story that has little to do with the product itself — emotion, aspiration, insecurity, identity. Dr. Jasleen Rana, who holds a PhD in Consumer Psychology and teaches Marketing at JIMS Kalkaji, moves past the question of what we buy to the more revealing one why. Through brand archetypes, hidden motivations, and everyday examples — choosing one coffee shop over another, paying more for a brand that does exactly what a cheaper one does — this interactive session decodes the psychological triggers behind consumer choice, and what those choices reveal about identity, belonging, and self-image.22nd October: Shubham YadavWhat if ordinary citizens believed they had something to teach the members of the Constituent Assembly? Shubham Yadav, a Senior Research Fellow at JNU's Zakir Husain Centre for Educational Studies, argues that India's Constitution wasn't shaped by elites alone — it emerged from a running exchange in which both "the people" and "the makers" wanted to instruct each other on what the new nation should be. Framed as a conversation rather than a lecture, the session traces that two-way pedagogy, and what it reveals about how theConstitution actually came to be built.

name: Tughlaqabad: Rise and Fall of a Dynasty
description: Rising dramatically from the rocky landscape of southern Delhi, Tughlaqabad stands as one of the most ambitious and haunting experiments in medieval urban history. Built in the fourteenth century by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, the vast fortified city marked the beginning of the Tughlaq dynasty and reflected a new architectural language defined by massive walls, sloping fortifications and an imposing sense of military power. Yet the city that was conceived to embody permanence would itself become closely associated with decline and abandonment.This walk explores the rise and fall of the Tughlaq dynasty through the extraordinary remains of Tughlaqabad and its surrounding landscape. Participants trace the vision behind this ambitious capital while uncovering the stories of Adilabad Fort, Nai ka Kot and the political and architectural developments that shaped the dynasty's early years. The experience culminates at the tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, one of the earliest and most distinctive monuments of Tughlaq architecture, where its design is explored in connection with the earlier tomb of Zafar Khan and the architectural ideas that preceded the Tughlaqs.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Tughlaqabad and the emergence of the Tughlaq dynasty in fourteenth-century Delhi.Explore Tughlaqabad Fort and understand Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's extraordinary vision of creating a vast fortified capital.Examine the distinctive military architecture of the fort, including its massive defensive walls, sloping bastions and strategic relationship with the surrounding rocky landscape.Discuss the rise of the Tughlaq dynasty and the circumstances that eventually contributed to the decline and abandonment of this ambitious imperial city.Explore the story and significance of Adilabad Fort and understand its relationship with the larger fortified landscape of Tughlaqabad.Discuss Nai ka Kot and its place within the wider story of Delhi's medieval defensive and urban landscape.Visit the tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq and examine one of the earliest examples of the architectural style that would come to define the Tughlaq period.Compare its architectural ideas with the earlier tomb of Zafar Khan, exploring the transition in tomb architecture and the developments that preceded the distinctive Tughlaq style.Conclude with a discussion on the ambitions, achievements and eventual decline of the Tughlaq dynasty, and how Tughlaqabad continues to preserve the memory of one of medieval Delhi's most dramatic experiments in imperial city-building.Key Themes & Highlights Rise of the Tughlaq DynastyTughlaqabad FortMedieval military architectureRise and fall of an imperial capitalAdilabad FortNai ka KotGhiyasuddin Tughlaq's TombEvolution of Tughlaq architectureConnection with Zafar Khan's TombDelhi Sultanate politics and power

name: Say Less: A Field Guide To Being Watched
description: About the LectureIs there a way to be seen that doesn't cost you your voice? Or was this trade always built into the system?You don't need to be arrested to stop speaking. You just need to suspect someone might be watching. After the 2013 Snowden revelations, researchers found a measurable drop in Wikipedia views of sensitive topics. No one was punished for reading an article. People simply stopped.This lecture is a field guide to being watched today. It covers the state with facial recognition and a database to match it against, the platforms built for advertising that can identify you from your own digital trail, and the quietest kind of all: the friend who screenshots, the forward, being recognised by someone you know. Along the way, we'll look at why visibility alone can be enough to change how we behave, and what that means for how freely any of us really speak.The session explores:Three ways of being watched: institutional, platform and lateral (peer) surveillanceThe panopticon: why the possibility of being watched does the work, not the watching itselfSocial sorting: how surveillance judges the category you've been placed in, not youThe chilling effect, and the evidence that it's more than a metaphorAbout the SpeakerSoumya Singh Chauhan is an Assistant Professor at O.P. Jindal Global University, where she is also pursuing her PhD on state data collection practices. Her research interests lie in privacy, surveillance and intellectual property law, and she teaches a surveillance elective at the university. When she's not thinking about the deep dystopia we live in, she zooms in: writing poetry, making art, or learning dance and music. A real escape would be to zoom out and finally pursue her as-yet-unsatiated interest in astronomy. Don't ask her anything about it right now; she knows nothing.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Delhi Ridge: From Empires to the Uprising
description: Long before Delhi expanded into the metropolis we know today, a rocky ridge defined its geography, protected its settlements, and silently witnessed the rise and fall of empires. Delhi Ridge: From Empires to the Uprising explores this remarkable landscape where natural history and human history have remained inseparable for more than two thousand years. name: How Indians Became Indian-Americans
description: About the LectureIn 1923, what did it take for an Indian man to be legally counted as "American"?Step inside one of the strangest, highest-stakes legal battles in modern history: United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind. At a time when American citizenship was limited to white people and people of African descent, a Sikh man went to the US Supreme Court to argue that he belonged. The Court responded by changing its own rules, overnight shifting the legal definition of "whiteness" from scientific classification to "common man" prejudice, to keep South Asians out.Lawyer and historian Vishwajeet Deshmukh has worked through archives in India, the United States and the United Kingdom to uncover the hidden layers of the case. Thind's argument, often criticised as promoting caste supremacy, turns out to have been a brilliant, desperate litigation strategy devised by the Ghadar Party, a radical, secular and explicitly anti-caste revolutionary movement. And behind the American courtroom, the British Empire was pulling strings. Terrified that Indian revolutionaries would secure US passports and immunity from British arrest, colonial spies used global surveillance to make sure South Asians were stripped of citizenship.With birthright citizenship back before the US Supreme Court, this story of identity, secret intelligence and a global fight over who gets to belong feels newly urgent.The session explores:How Indians in the United States used the law to fight for citizenship in the 1920sHow the US Supreme Court rewrote the definition of "whiteness" to exclude South AsiansThe Ghadar Party's hidden hand in Thind's legal strategyHow British intelligence shaped the outcome of an American court caseAbout the SpeakerVishwajeet Deshmukh is a lawyer and historian whose work focuses on how law creates identities and how legal systems shape them. He has written on the legal history of Anglo-Indians, Jews and South Asian Americans. He holds an LLM from Harvard Law School with a focus on legal history, has spoken at TEDx, and has been a guest lecturer at National Law University Delhi, National Law University Ranchi and Government Law College, Mumbai. He received the Tata Trusts Grant from the 1947 Partition Archive and Ashoka University for his research on the impact of Partition on minorities in India and Pakistan, and the Sutin Prize and Jeannie Shawl Prize from JURIST, University of Pittsburgh. He has clerked at the Bombay High Court and worked as an archival researcher at ETH Zürich.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive, unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Red Fort: The Making of Shahjahanabad
description: More than a royal residence, the Red Fort was the heart of Shahjahanabad.This walk explores the Red Fort as a carefully designed imperial world where architecture, ceremony, water and power came together to express the grandeur of the Mughal Empire. Participants journey through its surviving palaces, audience halls and gardens to understand how the emperor's authority was physically staged and experienced within the fort. From the public spectacle of the Diwan-i-Aam to the private elegance of the imperial apartments, every space reveals a different aspect of Mughal courtly life.The experience also explores the transformation of the fort across centuries, from the glory of Shah Jahan's reign to the changing political fortunes of the Mughal Empire and the events that reshaped its identity in the colonial period. Through architecture and storytelling, the walk reveals the Red Fort not simply as a monument, but as the centre of an imperial vision that once shaped the life and identity of an entire city.Detailed Flow of WalkIntroduction to Shah Jahan's decision to establish Shahjahanabad and the role of the Red Fort as the political and ceremonial heart of the new Mughal capital.Enter the fort and examine its strategic location, monumental architecture and relationship with the wider city of Shahjahanabad.Explore the Diwan-i-Aam and understand the rituals of Mughal kingship, public audiences and the carefully designed relationship between the emperor and his subjects.Visit the Diwan-i-Khas and examine the world of imperial privilege, courtly culture and the political symbolism expressed through its extraordinary architecture.Trace the Nahr-i-Bihisht, or Stream of Paradise, and understand the importance of water in Mughal architecture, garden design and ideas of paradise.Explore the imperial residential spaces and discuss the daily life, privacy and ceremonial practices of the Mughal court.Examine the architectural language of the Red Fort and understand how materials, ornamentation, gardens and water were brought together to create an idealised imperial landscape.Discuss the changing fortunes of the Mughal Empire and the transformation of the fort as imperial power gradually declined.Conclude with the later history and legacy of the Red Fort, reflecting on how a seventeenth-century imperial palace became one of the most powerful symbols of Delhi and India's historical memory.Key Themes & Highlights Shah Jahan and the making of ShahjahanabadMughal imperial architectureArchitecture of powerRoyal court and ceremonyDiwan-i-Aam and Diwan-i-KhasImperial palaces and private lifeWater architecture and the Nahr-i-BihishtMughal gardens and aestheticsDecline of Mughal powerTransformation of the Red Fort through history
